name: Russell's judgment that substituting Aristotle for Plato/Augustine was a Christian mistake
plain_explanation: Russell argues that because Plato's temperament was inherently more religious than Aristotle's, and because Christian theology had from nearly its beginning been adapted to Platonism (largely via Augustine), the thirteenth-century triumph of Aristotle (secured by Albertus Magnus and Aquinas) was, from the Church's own point of view, a poor trade -- even though, ironically, it also unintentionally prepared the way for a later 'return from Platonic dreaming to scientific observation.'
precise_definition: Russell's direct evaluative claim, made in his own voice, that the scholastic elevation of Aristotle above Plato and Augustine as the 'supreme authority after Scripture and the Church' weakened rather than strengthened Christian theology's natural religious temperament, notwithstanding its unintended long-term benefit of nudging Western thought toward empirical observation.
why_it_mattered: This is one of the clearest instances in the whole book of Russell stepping outside historical narration to render a first-person philosophical-theological verdict, and it retrospectively frames his critical treatment of Aquinas in Chapter XIII.
historical_origin: Stated directly by Russell in this chapter's opening retrospective section.
examples: Plato's teaching that knowledge is not perception but a kind of reminiscent vision, contrasted with Aristotle's greater empiricism
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell credits this same Aristotelian shift, 'little though he intended it,' with Aquinas preparing the way for the eventual return to scientific observation -- a double-edged legacy.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly a claim about the fit between a philosophical system and a religious tradition's own temperament.
